title: Microwave dielectric properties of LiNbO$_{\mathbf{3}}$ and AlN at millikelvin temperatures and single-photon power
authors: Alessandro Reineri, Francesco Crisa, Akshay Murthy, Maithlee Shinde, Daniel Bafia, Changqing Wang, Tanay Roy, Alexander Romanenko, John Zasadzinski, Anna Grassellino, Silvia Zorzetti
abstract: Efficient bidirectional microwave optical photon conversion is a key capability for scaling superconducting quantum processors into distributed networks. However, achieving the necessary conversion efficiency requires filling a critical knowledge gap in understanding the loss mechanisms of electro optic materials. Here, we characterize the microwave properties of single crystal bulk LiNbO3 and AlN over a broad range of powers, down to single photon levels, and spanning from millikelvin temperatures to above 1K. We demonstrate that both materials exhibit two level systems (TLS) behavior, while piezoelectric related losses are excluded. We show that TLS induced dissipation is predominantly localized on the surface rather than being an intrinsic bulk property, a result further corroborated by room temperature 3D XPS and time of flight SIMS analyses. These findings provide useful insights to engineer hybrid architectures that integrate bulk electro optic crystals within superconducting cavities, proving that microwave quality factors compatible with high efficiency microwave optical transduction are within reach.
summary: This experimental study characterizes the microwave dielectric losses in $	ext{LiNbO}_3$ and $	ext{AlN}$ crystals down to single-photon levels at millikelvin temperatures. By analyzing power and temperature dependencies, the authors determined that losses are primarily due to surface-localized Two-Level Systems (TLS), not intrinsic bulk properties. These findings provide crucial material science guidance for engineering high-efficiency quantum transduction interfaces.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the microwave dielectric properties of $	ext{LiNbO}_3$ and $	ext{AlN}$ at millikelvin temperatures and single-photon power to understand loss mechanisms for efficient bidirectional microwave-optical photon conversion.
main_result: The research found that microwave losses are dominated by Two-Level Systems (TLS) localized on the surface rather than being an intrinsic bulk property, confirming that high-efficiency transduction is achievable.
method: The authors used superconducting radiofrequency (SRF) cavity measurements, performing power and temperature sweeps while fitting the $S_{11}$ data to extract quality factors ($Q_0$).
model_or_system: The physical system involves single-crystal bulk $	ext{LiNbO}_3$ and $	ext{AlN}$ placed within a superconducting cavity cooled to millikelvin temperatures. The analysis models loss contributions from TLS, power-dependent effects, and temperature-dependent superconducting losses.
key_observables: Internal microwave quality factor ($Q_0$), loss tangent ($	an \delta_m$), and the dependence of $Q_0$ on microwave power and temperature.
important_parameters: Millikelvin temperatures (down to 10 mK), single-photon power levels, and the critical power for TLS saturation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed losses are dominated by near-surface defects, which is corroborated by complementary XPS and ToF-SIMS depth profiling analyses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cavity architecture, field distribution for TM and TE modes, and power sweeps showing the model fits for $Q_0$ dependence on input power for both materials.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem definition (need for efficient transduction) $ightarrow$ experimental setup (SRF cavity measurements) $ightarrow$ detailed analysis (power/temperature sweeps using multi-component fitting models) $ightarrow$ physical interpretation (surface vs. bulk losses) $ightarrow$ conclusion regarding material engineering.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical hardware bottleneck—material loss—for scaling superconducting quantum processors into distributed quantum networks by characterizing electro-optic materials at the quantum limit.
